steps.title: Electromagnetic induction
steps.body: The process of inducing a potential difference (and current if the circuit is complete) in a conductor by moving it through a magnetic field, or by changing the magnetic field around a conductor.

steps.title: Generator effect
steps.body: When a wire moves through a magnetic field (or a magnetic field changes through a coil), a potential difference is induced. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current flows. This is the opposite of the motor effect.

steps.title: Transformer
steps.body: A device that changes the voltage of an alternating current. It consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on the same iron core. Transformers only work with AC.

steps.title: Step-up transformer
steps.body: A transformer that increases the voltage (more turns on the secondary coil than the primary).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Example 1: Transformer turns calculation A step-down transformer has 2000 turns on the primary coil and 100 turns on the secondary coil. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage. Solution: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns 230 / Vs = 2000 / 100 = 20 Vs = 230 / 20 = 11.5 V Example 2: Step-up transformer A step-up transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 10,000 turns on the secondary. The input voltage is 25,000 V. Calculate the output voltage. Solution: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns 25000 / Vs = 500 / 10000 = 0.05 Vs = 25000 / 0.05 = 500,000 V (500 kV) Example 3: Transformer current calculation A 100% efficient transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V and a secondary voltage of 11.5 V. The primary current is 0.2 A. Calculate the secondary current. steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: For electromagnetic induction, remember: movement or change is needed. A stationary wire in a constant field produces no induced PD. Know the difference between slip rings (alternator/AC) and split ring commutator (dynamo/DC) — this is a very common question. In transformer calculations, always set up the ratio Vp/Vs = Np/Ns carefully — make sure primary values are on one side and secondary on the other. For National Grid questions, link: high voltage → low current → less heat loss (P = I2R). Always mention the I2R equation. Transformers are never 100% efficient in reality — some energy is lost as heat in the coils and core. But for calculations, assume 100% efficiency unless told otherwise.
